The atlas lists all 1253 graphs on up to seven nodes once each, up to isomorphism, ordered by node count, then edge count, then degree sequence." width="100%"} Ronald C. Read and Robin J. Wilson's "An Atlas of Graphs" (Oxford University Press, 1998) lists all 1253 graphs with up to seven nodes, up to isomorphism, numbered `0` to `1252` in a fixed order: by number of nodes, then by number of edges, then by degree sequence, then by number of automorphisms. So graph `0` is the empty graph, `1` a single node, `2` and `3` the two graphs on two nodes, and `208` to `1252` the 1044 graphs on seven nodes. This method adds one of them with exactly the nodes and edges NetworkX's `graph_atlas()` gives. `atlas_graphs()` returns them all. In a directed graph every edge points from the earlier-created node to the later one. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. The atlas is useful for: - exhaustively testing a conjecture or an algorithm on every small graph - looking up small graphs by their standard atlas number - finding small counterexamples ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [index]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Atlas number, from `0` to `1252`. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `index=` is outside `0` to `1252`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Graph 6 is the path on three nodes, and graph 7 the triangle: ::: {#a031f2b1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec ec.Graph().add_atlas_graph(6).get_edges_str_repr(), ec.Graph().add_atlas_graph(7).get_edges_str_repr() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (['1--2', '1--3'], ['1--2', '1--3', '2--3']) ``` ::: ::: The last graph in the atlas is the complete graph on seven nodes: ::: {#75bad829 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} last = ec.Graph().add_atlas_graph(1252) last.count_nodes(), last.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (7, 21) ``` ::: :::
